newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek premier backs missile deployment in Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Greek premier backs missile deployment in Cyprus.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis said on Friday Athens backed a Cypriot government decision to deploy Russian missiles in Cyprus which has heightened tensions in the eastern Mediterranean.
"We stressed Greece's full support to the struggle of the Cypriot people and our clear backing for Cyprus' defence effort," Simitis said after a meeting with Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides.
Cyprus announced this month it was buying S-300 anti-aircraft missiles from Russia and Turkey quickly said it would strike if necessary to ensure they were never deployed.
"It is the right of the Cypriot democracy to buy the arms it deems necessary," Clerides said. "On this matter we don't accept any suggestions."

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded in response to a Greek Cypriot coup engineered by a military junta then ruling Greece. Ankara maintains some 30,000 troops in a self-declared Turkish Cypriot state in the north.
Greece and Cyprus signed a military cooperation pact in 1993 and have worked to coordinate military strategy, exercises and equipment.
"The defence cooperation between Greece and Cyprus is a steady choice of the two governments," Simitis said.
He said Athens wanted a peaceful reunification of Cyprus based on United Nations proposals and called on the international community to stop Ankara's threats to strike if the missiles were deployed.
Washington, fearing another crisis between NATO allies Greece and Turkey, sent State Department envoy Carey Cavanaugh to Nicosia, Athens and Ankara in an effort to ease the tension.

The United States has sharply criticised the missile purchase and said it was a destabilising mistake. But it also said that any strike by Turkey was unacceptable and that Ankara should stop threatening the use of force.
Turkey fears that S-300s would compromise its air superiority in the region.
Cavanaugh ended his trip to the region in Ankara on Thursday saying a potential crisis had been averted after a promise by Clerides that the S-300s would not be installed for 16 months.
Turkey has discounted Cavanaugh's optimism, saying the 16 months is meaningless because the missiles were not due to be delivered from Russia until mid-1998 anyway.
